clinicalPearls: Bacterial vaginosis reflects a shift in the vaginal microbiome away from protective lactobacilli toward an overgrowth of anaerobes rather than a single infecting pathogen
The characteristic feature is a thin, homogeneous, greyish-white discharge with a fishy odour that is often most noticeable after intercourse
It is typically not associated with significant inflammation, so vulval itching and soreness are usually mild or absent, distinguishing it from candidiasis and trichomoniasis
Clinical diagnosis using the Amsel criteria combines discharge characteristics, raised vaginal pH, a positive whiff test with potassium hydroxide, and clue cells on microscopy
Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria and are a hallmark microscopic finding
Treatment targets anaerobes with agents such as metronidazole or clindamycin, but recurrence is common and reflects failure to re-establish a lactobacillus-dominant flora
In pregnancy it is associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, late miscarriage, and postpartum endometritis, so symptomatic pregnant women are treated
It also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections including HIV and to post-procedural pelvic infection
reference.pathophysiology: The healthy vagina is dominated by lactobacilli that produce lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide, maintaining an acidic environment that suppresses other organisms. In bacterial vaginosis this population is depleted and replaced by a polymicrobial overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Atopobium, often organised into a biofilm on the epithelium. The resulting rise in vaginal pH and production of amines generates the typical odour and discharge, while the biofilm contributes to treatment resistance and recurrence.
additionalDifferentials: Retained foreign body such as a tampon
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of vaginal pH, which is typically elevated above 4.5
Whiff (amine) test with potassium hydroxide to detect a fishy odour
Saline wet-mount microscopy for clue cells and reduced lactobacilli
Gram stain scoring of vaginal flora where laboratory diagnosis is used
Testing for co-existing sexually transmitted infections when risk factors are present
redFlags: Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy given the association with preterm birth and miscarriage
Signs of ascending infection such as pelvic pain, fever, or cervical motion tenderness suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease
Bacterial vaginosis before termination or intrauterine procedures, increasing post-procedure infection risk
Persistent atypical discharge not responding to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Coexisting features of a sexually transmitted infection
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually respond well to appropriate antibiotic therapy, but recurrence within months is frequent because the protective lactobacillus flora and the biofilm are difficult to eradicate permanently. It is not itself a serious infection but its associations with adverse pregnancy outcomes, post-procedural infection, and enhanced susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections give it clinical importance.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for candidiasis and treating with antifungals
Overtreating asymptomatic women outside pregnancy or pre-procedure settings
Failing to consider it in recurrent or malodorous discharge with minimal inflammation
Not screening for concurrent sexually transmitted infections when risk exists
Overlooking its role in preterm birth in symptomatic pregnant women
management: Treat symptomatic infection with an anti-anaerobic antibiotic, either oral or intravaginal metronidazole or intravaginal clindamycin
Advise avoidance of alcohol during and shortly after metronidazole because of a disulfiram-like reaction
Advise against vaginal douching and use of irritant products to help restore lactobacillus-dominant flora
Treat symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy given the association with preterm birth and late miscarriage
For frequent recurrence, offer suppressive intravaginal metronidazole and consider lactobacillus-restoring or vaginal-pH-lowering measures
Test for co-existing sexually transmitted infections when risk factors are present
